newsitem.title: USA: Brent even in late US trade, foreign crudes steady.
newsitem.headline: Brent even in late US trade, foreign crudes steady.

text.p: North Sea Brent traded even to slightly lower in late U.S. trading Friday although activity was light heading into the weekend, traders said.
A series of partial paper Brents for April traded at $21.80/21.82/21.84/21.86 a barrel, compared to $21.85 at the IPE settlement.
Feb/March Brent changed hands twice at 37 cents, while March/April traded twice at 41 cents, traders said.

The Gulf Coast continues to attract a plethora of foreign crudes. Transatlantic trade is brisk, thanks to the open arbitrage between West Texas Intermediate/Cushing and Brent, which stood around $1.70-80 a barrel.
Three companies are showing Brents into the Gulf Coast for the first half of February around March WTI minus 30 cents a barrel delivered, traders said.
Traders noted, however, that the Gulf probably has room for just two million barrels in that time period, not enough to accommodate all the offers.
"Buying interest is around minus 40-50 cents," one seller said. "The Gulf is confident is can get those numbers."

In neighboring Latin America, activity was moderate. Chile's state-owned oil company Empresa Nacional del Petroleo (ENAP) bought a cargo each of Oriente and West African crude in the company's regular crude tender for 960,000 barrels, trade sources said.
Traders said ENAP bought Angolan Palanca, but this could not be confirmed.
Chile has frequently purchased Palanca as well as other West African crudes such as Nigerian Escravos.
Elsewhere, Argentina's YPF was close to selling 950,000 barrels of Canadon Seco loading February 24-25, traders said.
Traders noted that the Gulf Coast is well-supplied with sour crudes as a result of rising Mexican and Venezuelan flows.
